title: Direct inguinal operative anatomy

cues.phrase: no moving sac follows the cord
cues.why: Directly negates the sac-repair competitor; the remaining operative choice repeats the affected wall.

cues.phrase: a broad bulge displaces the canal wall
cues.why: The sole positive moving structure matches 'inguinal-wall reinforcement'; combined with explicit sac exclusion and work interruption, it supplies an elimination route.

fairness: The key is directionally defensible for a symptomatic direct defect, but the operative alternatives are not cleanly exclusive: a real inguinal repair can inspect the deep ring and reinforce the posterior wall. This is largely anatomy recognition followed by its corresponding repair label, too easy for routine PGY-2/3 use.

Importance: high-yield groin anatomy and symptomatic-hernia management. Realism: clinic presentation is credible; framing repair as wall reinforcement versus sac repair oversimplifies actual adult repair planning.
suggestions: Use distinct whole operative or observation plans, with a real patient-specific reason to distinguish them. Do not imply posterior-wall reinforcement is exclusive to direct hernias.

Retain symptom burden and dynamic findings, but remove the redundant explicit sac negation if the revised alternatives remain fairly distinguishable. A labelled original anatomy exhibit would better test spatial interpretation.

title: Postoperative distension cross-sectional assessment

cues.phrase: Contrast CT
cues.why: An already completed CT makes the same undifferentiated CT option disposable; no changed protocol or new question explains repeating it.

fairness: Recurrent high-amylase fluid after pancreatic-neck surgery requires recognition of a duct-related problem and then selection of duct assessment. MRCP is plausible, but the task asks what should guide the next drainage plan without resolving diagnostic mapping versus therapeutic ERCP; both may be defensible depending on continuity and intervention intent.

Importance: high for postoperative pancreatic complications. Realism: the hospital-record review is plausible, but timing, duct anatomy already known, and the planned drainage decision are insufficiently specified. No source verification was performed in this offline review.
suggestions: State the unresolved duct question and whether noninvasive anatomical mapping or a potentially therapeutic duct intervention is being selected. Supply existing duct information and relevant procedural constraints without announcing the preferred modality.
Replace generic repeat CT with a credible distinct investigation, or give an actual acquisition defect that makes repeat CT a competitor.

title: Postoperative fluid composition

cues.phrase: tenderness and fever
cues.why: Together with numerous neutrophils, this strongly preselects the culture half of the option matrix, leaving cytology as an obvious wrong-stage substitute.

cues.phrase: beside the pancreatic tail
cues.why: Direct organ-to-assay association selects amylase over bilirubin; the key is assembled from two elementary associations rather than a difficult fluid interpretation.

fairness: The balanced component frequencies prevent majority-component convergence, and the combined triglyceride/amylase/culture request is defensible. However, triglycerides are common to every choice, so the cloudy/oily-fluid material is not discriminating. This is parallel assay recall, too easy for residents.

Importance: postoperative leak and infected-collection evaluation are high-yield. Realism: mixed lymphatic/pancreatic/infectious processes are plausible; the selected assay contrasts are less credible than the clinical problem.
suggestions: Make an actual discordant fluid result or collection trajectory change the next action. Compare plausible leak/infection workups at the same stage, rather than replacing necessary culture with cytology.
Retain fever and safety findings; change the distractors instead of hiding infection.

title: Nutrition for postoperative chylous leakage

cues.phrase: To regain weight he added olive-oil drinks and full-fat milk; drain output rose afterward
cues.why: Rehearses the dietary-fat mechanism and directly points to the only fat-restriction option.

cues.phrase: Meals and supplements supply the assessed energy and protein requirement
cues.why: Along with stable weight, electrolytes and meal tolerance, this systematically removes the rationale for both artificial-feeding alternatives.

cues.phrase: Meals pass without vomiting or distension; the collection remains drained
cues.why: Adds another explicit route-feasibility exclusion after adequate oral intake has already been established.

fairness: The oral fat-modification key is plausible, but the competitor routes are not close choices given repeatedly declared oral adequacy. Fat-type recall is the remaining step; too easy for PGY-2/3.

Importance: useful postoperative nutrition concept. Realism: plausible dietary exacerbation, but the nutrition prescription is abbreviated and sustained nutritional adequacy would need clinical follow-up.
suggestions: Give actual intake/output and response observations that leave more than one nutrition strategy credible, then test a consequential change in route or composition.
Remove repeated adequacy assurances; retain enough intake and physiological information to choose safely.

title: Nutrition during prolonged postoperative ileus

cues.phrase: the nutrition team was planning additional delivery
cues.why: Previews supplementation, favoring 'Supplemental PN' over 'Exclusive PN' before the learner integrates the feeding record.

cues.phrase: thiamine after hypophosphatemia
cues.why: Both distractors advertise delayed prophylaxis after a complication. A general prevention-before-harm heuristic can eliminate half the matrix.

fairness: Severe nutritional depletion with inadequate but tolerated enteral delivery supports a genuine route-plus-refeeding decision. Normal baseline electrolytes do not remove the need to consider refeeding risk. The key is plausible, but 'Supplemental PN and thiamine before escalation' is incomplete as a nutrition-start plan: it does not specify cautious delivery or monitoring, and could be read as immediate full replacement.

Importance: high-yield perioperative nutrition and refeeding safety. Realism: prolonged postoperative dysfunction is plausible; the already declared additional-delivery plan weakens independent assessment.
suggestions: Remove the prospective team decision and use the observed delivery/tolerance record.

Compare complete start/escalation plans with appropriate monitoring and credible errors in energy advancement or route choice; avoid waiting-for-hypophosphatemia wording as the principal distractor. Do not invent a dosing threshold.

title: Mesh after a controlled enterotomy
fairness: One defensible best option among those offered: interpret controlled contamination and feasible retromuscular separation, then choose an appropriate mesh material. The small amount of suctioned fluid and closure observations are decision-critical rather than gratuitous reassurance. No exploitable grammar, length or convergence cue identified.

Importance: high-yield and practically consequential hernia-reconstruction judgment. Realism: suitable as retrospective hospital operative-record review, not an intervention performed in clinic. Implant choice remains clinician-dependent; this editorial PASS is not clinical approval or fresh evidence verification.
suggestions: Preserve the controlled-contamination and fascial-closure boundaries in any reuse; do not generalize this key to uncontrolled contamination or every implant position.

title: Meckel resection extent

cues.phrase: left a slit-like lumen
cues.why: Describes the local closure as mechanically unacceptable in ordinary language, eliminating the principal competing operation before a resident must reason about extent.

cues.phrase: The wall defect was centered at the diverticular base rather than the distal tip
cues.why: Repeats the earlier base/adjacent-wall involvement and reiterates why limited diverticulectomy is wrong.

fairness: Segmental resection is defensible given diseased adjacent ileum and the described closure narrowing. These findings should not be hidden if they truly occurred, but they make the supplied alternatives too easy. The apparent second step is largely supplied by the failed closure trial.

Importance: high-yield bowel-preserving resection decisions. Realism: an operative record can describe a closure assessment, but a cut test edge and trial closure before selecting extent make the simulated chronology awkward.
suggestions: Use a coherent pre-resection anatomical record and compare credible extents of resection. If an actual failed local closure is retained, accept this as an easy safety/application item only with independent basic-role approval.
Remove the duplicate distribution row and make the remaining anatomy, not a narrated failed option, determine the operation.

title: Celiac serology when IgA is deficient
fairness: The learner must recognize two independent limitations of the negative test: absent IgA and testing after gluten removal. The balanced panel/diet matrix does not yield the key through majority convergence. Laboratory labels are necessary data, not sufficient nonmedical cues to the correct exposure plan.

Importance: useful nutritional/malabsorption workup for general surgery, though less central than operative emergencies. Realism: a nutrition-clinic referral is credible. The key should be interpreted as a supervised diagnostic plan, not unsupervised dietary challenge instructions; no dose or duration is validated here.
suggestions: Preserve both assay-validity and diet-exposure issues. In clinical feedback clarify supervised reintroduction and subsequent diagnostic assessment without implying serology alone always completes diagnosis.

title: Celiac testing after gluten withdrawal

cues.phrase: asks whether every diagnostic pathway requires repeating that experience
cues.why: The patient explicitly asks to avoid challenge; only HLA-before-challenge offers an obvious challenge-sparing sequence, paraphrasing the key's rationale.

fairness: Recognizing invalid negative studies during restriction and the potential exclusion value of HLA testing is meaningful. HLA-first is reasonable in this context, but supervised challenge is also a legitimate diagnostic sequence if accepted; the patient's question is not an explicit decision or contraindication. The optimal sequence should not rest solely on suggestive preference wording.
Importance: useful but overlaps heavily with the other celiac testing items. Realism: credible consultation about an uncertain lifelong diagnosis.
suggestions: Describe the prior challenge response neutrally and state an actual agreed constraint if it is essential. Compare equally feasible diagnostic sequences under that constraint.
Avoid a patient question that restates the intended benefit of the only keyed test. Consider merging overlapping celiac invalid-test objectives through manager review.

title: Positive celiac susceptibility typing

cues.phrase: no prior IgA-based celiac serology is listed
cues.why: Names the missing assay family; the key supplies it.

cues.phrase: Which diagnostic plan should precede Olivia Park's dietary prescription?
cues.why: The task's explicit before-diet ordering disfavors the option that obtains the same test 'after gluten withdrawal' without requiring interpretation of HLA or IgG.

fairness: tTG-IgA during ongoing gluten exposure is a defensible next blood test in an IgA-sufficient patient. The positive HLA and IgG details can be ignored once the omitted IgA test is named; too easy for residents. The broad 'diagnostic plan' task also leaves biopsy-based evaluation outside the offered comparison.

Importance: useful serology interpretation, but largely duplicates the neighboring celiac items. Realism: commercial testing can create this problem; the current options reduce it to a missing-test exercise.
suggestions: Remove the named-omission sentence and use an actual test record requiring interpretation.
Ask a specific next testing decision and compare credible assay/biopsy strategies with patient-specific reasons. Keep gluten exposure information because it is necessary for test validity.

title: HCC tumor burden versus liver resection suitability
fairness: The small solitary tumor tempts local treatment, while recurrent ascites and portal-hypertension findings require integration of liver disease with tumor burden. Transplant-center assessment is a defensible priority; ablation can still have a bridging role and is not categorically wrong treatment.

Importance: high-yield HCC treatment planning. Realism: credible clinic referral, and 'assessment' appropriately avoids declaring transplant eligibility from incomplete data. No conspicuous option-style or nonmedical cue identified.
suggestions: Keep the task as prioritizing assessment rather than asserting transplantation must occur. Preserve the distinction between the ultimate pathway and possible bridging local treatment.

title: Structural assessment before gastric emptying
fairness: The interrupted examination and prepyloric-only histology leave an irregular pyloric narrowing unevaluated. Interpreting that sampling limitation and prioritizing targeted endoscopy over a motility study is a consequential two-step decision. Contrast passage does not by itself establish that the structural lesion is irrelevant.

Importance: high-yield differentiation of structural obstruction from diabetic dysmotility. Realism: decompression before re-evaluation is plausible. Repeat endoscopy needs an appropriate aspiration-risk/anesthetic plan, but absence of its technical details does not make the offered diagnostic ranking unfair.
suggestions: Preserve the exact site and adequacy distinctions; do not replace the raw record with 'inconclusive endoscopy' or a diagnosed obstruction label.

title: Reassessing nutrition after ileus resolves

cues.phrase: meet her assessed energy and protein needs on each of the last three days
cues.why: Supplies the nutritional-adequacy conclusion instead of requiring assessment, directly cueing PN withdrawal.

cues.phrase: Reduce PN; reduce separate fluid replacement
cues.why: Reducing replacement in the face of thirst, falling urine output, weight loss and rising creatinine is an obviously self-defeating distractor.

fairness: The intended distinction between nutritional delivery and replacement of stoma losses is important. However, recorded intake is not necessarily absorbed intake in a high-output ileostomy; the statement of dietary intake alone does not firmly establish independence from parenteral nutritional support. The combination of a supplied adequacy conclusion and a plainly inappropriate fluid reduction makes this too easy rather than genuinely integrative.

Importance: high-yield postoperative fluid/nutrition care. Realism: a clinic presentation with orthostasis and renal deterioration needs explicit current assessment and an appropriate setting for replacement.
suggestions: Provide a supported assessment of nutritional absorption/trajectory, relevant bowel context and the current volume problem without simply declaring requirements met.
Compare plausible fluid/electrolyte and nutrition prescriptions, keeping necessary replacement in all credible choices; avoid a distractor that deliberately worsens obvious depletion.

title: Incidental gallbladder muscle invasion

cues.phrase: the cystic-duct margin is free of tumor
cues.why: Directly removes the duct-stump re-excision option, leaving the familiar muscle-invasion versus surveillance rule.

cues.phrase: revised pathology
cues.why: Together with the original 'superficial' summary and newly emphasized smooth-muscle invasion, the task signals escalation; this is a weaker test-taking cue rather than proof of the key by itself.

fairness: HPB assessment for completion resection is defensible from the stated invasion and staging. Muscle involvement followed by its standard referral is a familiar recall chain, not two consequential inferences. No independent accepted basic role is visible.

Importance: high-yield incidental gallbladder cancer. Realism: plausible postoperative consultation, with useful functional context. The necessary margin result should not simply be deleted to make stump re-excision look viable.
This is a fresh difficulty concern about a frozen version, not authorization to alter it; the manager should adjudicate basic-role acceptance or a separately versioned revision.
suggestions: Preserve invasion and margin facts, but replace the explicitly excluded stump option with a credible competing plan at the same stage.
Introduce a real staging, specimen-adequacy or operative-suitability decision that changes the completion-resection pathway, supported by verified criteria.

title: Gastric cancer with adjacent-organ invasion

cues.phrase: the surgeon could not develop a plane through it
cues.why: Directly defeats 'Gastrectomy after pancreatic-plane separation'; the unsuccessful maneuver supplies the key distinction.

cues.phrase: No peritoneal deposits or other distant disease at operative assessment
cues.why: Repeated absence of distant disease weakens the sole palliative alternative, while the next row supplies an apparent resectability permission.

cues.phrase: proximal pancreatic division and gastric resection margins can be placed outside the bridge
cues.why: Rehearses feasibility of the only en-bloc operation rather than leaving a consequential planning inference.

fairness: En-bloc resection is plausible for a potentially curable inseparable malignant interface. Histological pancreatic involvement plus no plane plus apparently clearable anatomy makes the alternatives too easily eliminated; reduced thickening after treatment adds little discrimination. Overall operative suitability and oncologic strategy are not fully established, so this should not teach automatic multivisceral resection from anatomy alone.
Importance: high-yield oncologic principles. Realism: a retrospective operative record is plausible; the exact pre-treatment biopsy route and extent require clinician confirmation.
suggestions: Retain necessary oncologic anatomy but compare realistic remaining operations or sequencing choices. Do not use a maneuver already documented as impossible as the close alternative.
Either test a true treatment-response/resectability uncertainty with sufficient data or acknowledge this as basic en-bloc oncologic principle recall.

title: Mammographic mass morphology
fairness: The resident must integrate interval change, scar location and morphology rather than equating palpability or density with the most concerning target. New spiculation away from the scar makes B a defensible first priority. The growing palpable C may also require sampling; the task correctly asks priority rather than exclusivity.

Importance: high-yield breast imaging/clinical correlation. Realism: three targets in one encounter are somewhat constructed but clinically coherent. No nonmedical wording cue reliably identifies B; interpreting the morphology requires knowledge.
suggestions: Keep subsequent evaluation of C explicit in feedback so prioritization is not taught as dismissal. Do not call this an item that establishes only one lesion merits biopsy.

title: Calcification morphology and distribution
fairness: The learner must separate successful retrieval of some calcium from radiology-pathology concordance, then select repeat sampling of the unresolved suspicious group. A is defensible despite its clip and specimen-radiograph confirmation. The B and C matches are meaningful clinical correlations, not merely identical answer-label words.

Importance: high-yield breast biopsy adequacy and avoiding false reassurance. Realism: credible multidisciplinary record review. A repeat representative sampling strategy is plausible, although the exact repeat modality versus excision remains a clinical-team decision not fully tested by identical option modalities.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between calcium retrieval and representation of the suspicious morphology. Confirm the repeat vacuum approach clinically before release; do not infer that it is universally superior to excision in every discordant biopsy.

title: Palpable breast mass in the thirties
fairness: Persistent suspicious palpation at the correctly imaged site requires reconciling examination with negative imaging, then choosing tissue acquisition. The negative studies are essential to the misconception being tested and do not simply name the key. Palpation-guided core biopsy is a defensible best option if the focus can be reliably targeted, as the presentation implies.

Importance: high-yield breast assessment and prevention of false reassurance. Realism: credible clinic case. No major option length, category or convergence cue found; difficulty is likely toward the easier end of moderate.
suggestions: Remove the duplicate marker/probe statement in the exhibit if it contributes no additional acquisition detail. Preserve the correctly targeted imaging premise and clearly suspicious examination.

title: Benign phyllodes excision planning

cues.phrase: leaving the visible end of that extension in the cavity
cues.why: Names the retained target, directly selecting 'Focused re-excision of the retained segment'.

cues.phrase: A small solid continuation of the same contour remains at the recorded nipple-side cavity edge
cues.why: Repeats confirmation of the sole limited target; it does not create a competing interpretation.

cues.phrase: for a fixed 10-mm rim
cues.why: The rigid numeric formulation makes this alternative look dogmatic next to an apparently tailored key.

fairness: Removing documented gross residual benign phyllodes is plausible. However, focused segment removal versus a mandated circumferential rim or nipple-areolar sacrifice is an easy proportionality choice. The record does not show actual nipple involvement to make central excision competitive.

Importance: moderate; distinguishing gross residual tumor from a microscopic positive margin is useful, but this sits among many overlapping phyllodes items. Realism: retained visible tumor after an unplanned excision is possible; 'full specimen' should not imply that retained tissue itself was examined.
suggestions: Compare equally plausible completion strategies under a genuine uncertainty about residual extent or grade. Avoid making nipple removal a foil without anatomical justification.
Use one decisive residual-tumor observation rather than repeatedly naming the retained segment. Consider merging with the benign-margin scenario while preserving separate objectives if retained.

title: Benign phyllodes margin after excision

cues.phrase: no transection
cues.why: Together with intact excision and no residual mass, explicitly excludes the principal reason for further local removal.

cues.phrase: no residual mass
cues.why: Reinforces the simple surveillance-versus-more-treatment route; the radiation alternative is particularly weak for a benign lesion.

fairness: Surveillance can be defensible after intact benign-phyllodes excision with a microscopic involved margin, but this is a single management-rule item, too easy for routine resident difficulty. The necessary completeness data are appropriate clinically; the problem is the weak alternative set.

Importance: useful practice-changing distinction but narrow and duplicated by adjacent items. Realism: strong postoperative-clinic fit. This independent concern does not authorize changing a frozen passed version; manager adjudication is required before any revision.
suggestions: Preserve the frozen version and record the difficulty concern for the manager. Seek explicit basic-role acceptance or develop a separately versioned question with a genuine competing decision.
Replace radiation with a credible postoperative strategy, and make specimen completeness or discordant residual findings consequential rather than supplying an entirely reassuring summary.

title: Borderline phyllodes close-margin action

cues.phrase: a lateral re-excision was booked
cues.why: Supplies one required component before the question, making lateral surveillance look inconsistent with the existing plan.

cues.phrase: subsequently identified a malignant component
cues.why: The narrative upgrade strongly signals adding a face to the already planned lateral excision; the only additive plan is the key. This gives a shortcut around knowing the actual margin policy.

fairness: Updating grade and then applying a margin policy could be a useful two-step task. However, the unique ranking of 4-mm and 2-mm margins depends on the malignant-phyllodes re-excision recommendation being used; no policy is stated, and exact margin practices are not safely assumed universal. I am not asserting that the keyed plan is clinically incorrect.

Importance: moderate specialist breast relevance; exact grade-specific margin thresholds are narrower than the general principle. Realism: specialist pathology addenda are plausible, but the apparently unchanged measurements do not themselves supply a universally agreed surgical rule.
suggestions: Name a verified clinical margin policy or provide its relevant recommendation neutrally, then require application to an oriented specimen with a consequential planning choice.
Remove the already booked plan if it merely supplies a component. Compare credible plans without an option that monitors the closest margin while removing a wider one without another reason.

title: Malignant phyllodes close-margin action

cues.phrase: every other face is at least 10 mm clear
cues.why: Directly eliminates whole-cavity surgery.

cues.phrase: an uninterrupted pectoral fascial line
cues.why: Combined with normal muscle findings, explicitly argues against both alternatives, which both remove muscle.

cues.phrase: no focal extension from the cavity
cues.why: Further reiterates the exclusion of the shared muscle-resection component in both distractors.

fairness: The key is the only plan sparing apparently uninvolved muscle, so the option set can be solved by proportionality even without knowing phyllodes margin policy. Whether a 4-mm posterior margin needs re-excision requires an explicit supported policy or clinician adjudication; the task assumes that decision already occurred.

Importance: useful principle of targeted margin clearance, but narrow and overlapping with the other deep-plane items. Realism: anatomy is coherent; routine postoperative MRI for this decision needs a stated clinical reason rather than being added to manufacture complexity.
suggestions: Compare realistic posterior strategies, including an appropriate breast/fascia boundary and a clinically credible observation or re-excision alternative under a stated policy.
Do not make both distractors require muscle removal despite repeated absence of muscle involvement. Keep necessary anatomy and remove redundant exclusion statements.

title: Axillary surgery in phyllodes
fairness: Adequate targeting, represented nodal tissue, benign cellular findings and interval improvement require a concordance assessment before applying the phyllodes axillary-surgery principle. This is more than simply announcing a negative node. Surveillance is a defensible choice among the options; routine sentinel-node logic from epithelial breast cancer is a credible error.

Importance: useful breast-surgery distinction, although phyllodes is overrepresented in this batch. Realism: credible preoperative clinic review. No decisive nonmedical overlap or option-format cue identified; exact pathology interpretation still needs clinician sign-off.
suggestions: Preserve targeting adequacy and trajectory. Do not generalize this answer to a persistently enlarging or discordantly sampled node.

title: A suspicious node in phyllodes

cues.phrase: insufficient remaining tissue for the requested classification panel
cues.why: Reiterates the earlier exhausted-cell-block finding and advertises a tissue-volume solution; it weakens repeat aspiration before its on-site preparation advantage is considered.

fairness: Obtaining more material and choosing an acquisition route are meaningful decisions, but the supplied reason for FNA failure is exhaustion, not a demonstrated need for tissue architecture. Repeat FNA with on-site preparation may therefore be defensible. Core biopsy may be preferable, yet a node adjacent to the axillary vein also requires an identified safe needle path; its depth does not alone settle core versus excision.

Importance: useful diagnostic sampling principle, but the rare phyllodes-node framing adds specialist detail. Realism: indeterminate spindle-cell cytology is plausible; the exact feasibility and classification requirements are missing.
suggestions: State what the pathologist still needs, distinguishing architecture from more cells for ancillary tests. Provide neutral imaging observations establishing feasible acquisition routes.
Compare plans that each could meet the material requirement; remove the duplicate inadequacy sentence rather than concealing the actual failed study.

title: Borderline phyllodes operative margin target

cues.phrase: the wall nodule remains similar in size
cues.why: After successful fluid aspiration, the unchanged solid component directly identifies the only option obtaining tissue from the persisting target.

cues.phrase: Core biopsy of the cavity-wall nodule
cues.why: The key is the only new diagnostic acquisition of solid tissue; one competitor repeats fluid aspiration and the other is surveillance despite the task asking for an acquisition.

fairness: Core sampling of the persistent vascular solid nodule is defensible. Distinguishing an aspirated cavity from an unsampled nodule is important, but this version largely names the missing target and asks for its biopsy. Serial ultrasound also does not match 'diagnostic acquisition' as naturally as a tissue procedure.

Importance: high practical value for postoperative mass evaluation, but not specific to borderline phyllodes or a margin target. Realism: plausible clinic course; reassuring old blood does not establish the nature of the solid component.
suggestions: Ask a neutral next diagnostic plan and compare plausible solid-target acquisition strategies, or introduce an actual sampling-concordance problem rather than an obviously unsampled persistent nodule.
Remove redundant cavity-response detail if it does not change the decision. Consider consolidating with other adequacy/discordance items.

title: Malignant phyllodes operative margin target

cues.phrase: the underlying muscle sliding independently of the mass
cues.why: Pre-explains that muscle is separable, strongly eliminating the muscle-resection competitor.

cues.phrase: The mass reaches the fascial surface; no focal signal extension is seen within pectoralis
cues.why: Names fascia while explicitly excluding muscle; selecting the middle anatomical extent becomes a matching exercise.

cues.phrase: the deep component remains to be specified
cues.why: Adds task framing rather than new decision information.

fairness: Including fascia while preserving uninvolved muscle is plausible, but this is essentially one plane-selection rule with a clearly inadequate capsule-following foil and an excessive muscle-removal foil. Imaging contact is not proof of invasion, and the exact required deep margin should be clinically reviewed rather than implied by the wording.

Importance: moderate specialist value; substantial overlap with the posterior re-excision item. Realism: a breast-conserving deep-plane plan is credible, while contraction ultrasound as a routine discriminator needs clinician confirmation.
suggestions: Use a clinically realistic interface uncertainty with credible competing resections, supported by actual margin guidance. Avoid describing each distractor's anatomical disqualification.
Remove the operative-planning filler row. Merge overlapping deep-plane objectives if the manager finds no distinct consequential decision.

title: Phyllodes dissemination pattern
fairness: The learner must recognize that the pulmonary lesion could change distant staging and distinguish its origin from two prior cancers before committing to local curative surgery. Lung-target tissue is a defensible priority among the offered acquisitions. Other targets remain clinically important but cannot resolve the same distant-disease question.

Importance: high-value general oncologic staging reasoning despite a rare-tumor wrapper. Realism: multidisciplinary clinic planning is plausible. The item presumes a feasible pulmonary core procedure; technical accessibility and safety should be confirmed clinically, but the presented peripheral target does not create an obvious competing key.
suggestions: Preserve the two-prior-primary ambiguity and curative-intent decision. Do not teach that every peripheral lesion must be biopsied by this route regardless of procedural risk.

title: Overt renin-independent aldosterone production

cues.phrase: He wants surgery if unilateral disease is demonstrated.
cues.why: This legitimate preference supplies the need for lateralization; combined with the testing-only task it narrows the task before biochemical interpretation. It must be retained if needed for fairness, but should not be the only reason one option fits.

cues.phrase: CT-directed unilateral adrenalectomy planning
cues.why: A treatment-planning option is a category outlier in a task specifically asking for an endocrine testing pathway, permitting nonmedical elimination.

fairness: Interpreting an overt biochemical phenotype, deciding whether suppression testing adds value, and choosing lateralization is a genuine stretch decision. The exact immunoassay/renin-based omission criterion and applicable contemporary guidance were not externally verified; I do not claim the key is wrong. The presentation says medicines were 'managed' without revealing relevant handling, limiting independent assessment if assay validity is part of the test.

Importance: high-yield endocrine surgery; distinguishing CT anatomy from functional lateralization is practically important. Realism: plausible clinic workup. Preserve the frozen version pending manager adjudication of this fresh option-category concern.
suggestions: Make every choice a concrete testing sequence, for example contrasting suppression-plus-lateralization and lateralization-first pathways, without including surgery planning as the obvious non-test.
Verify the exact criterion and medication context before release. If medication preparation is not the objective, avoid making its unspecified handling carry a scored inference.

title: Factor assessment after an inhibitory mixing pattern
fairness: Immediate correction followed by loss of correction on incubation, a valid control and new bleeding support interpreting a time-dependent inhibitor pattern and selecting targeted factor/inhibitor testing. Factor VIII testing is present in all choices, so the distinguishing second assay must be considered. No unfair convergence or simple phrase-match key found.

Importance: high-yield perioperative bleeding assessment. Realism: plausible laboratory/hematology consultation. A mixing pattern alone is not definitive diagnosis, and lupus-anticoagulant testing may coexist in a wider workup; the offered targeted priority remains defensible.
suggestions: Retain the control and medication-interference checks; these establish assay interpretability. Keep feedback clear that follow-up testing, not the mixing study alone, establishes the diagnosis.

title: New swelling despite established lymphedema
fairness: The learner must reconcile acute whole-leg change with compressible examined veins, interpret asymmetric respiratory phasicity as a reason to assess more proximal venous disease, and select appropriate imaging coverage. The visible image was inspected and matches its description; it is explicitly a constructed, unscaled teaching trace.

Importance: high-yield recognition of a new process in a chronically swollen limb and limits of a negative duplex. Realism: credible clinic-to-urgent-investigation pathway. CT venous-phase imaging is a defensible choice among those offered, subject to patient-specific contrast suitability not assessed here.
suggestions: Preserve the acquisition territory and waveform comparison; do not replace them with a diagnosed iliac obstruction. Confirm clinical interpretation and imaging suitability before sign-off.

title: Symptom control versus thyroid-hormone production

cues.phrase: Slow pulse with lightheadedness; tremor no longer present
cues.why: Both distractors maintain propranolol while only the key reduces it. Recognizing the symptomatic slow pulse selects the entire answer without interpreting the thyroid tests.

cues.phrase: Maintain methimazole and reduce propranolol
cues.why: The key alone adjusts the symptom-control drug; the unbalanced component matrix bypasses the intended TSH-versus-free-hormone reasoning.

fairness: Reducing beta blockade is plausible given the current symptoms, and persistent low TSH need not mean persistent excess free hormone. However, the exact methimazole maintenance decision also depends on treatment interval, current dose and trend, which are not supplied. I am not declaring the offered key wrong; it is the best of an artificially weak set.
Importance: high-yield perioperative endocrine medication reasoning. Realism: plausible clinic follow-up, but breastfeeding is unused by all three options and adds no current discriminator.
suggestions: Include a credible competing plan that also reduces propranolol so the learner must interpret the thyroid trajectory to choose the methimazole action.
Provide the clinically needed treatment chronology and regimen, using verified values. Remove breastfeeding if it has no role in the revised decision.

title: IVC filter versus anticoagulation for a provoked DVT

cues.phrase: its proximal and distal limits are unchanged
cues.why: Along with decreasing tenderness and circumference, this explicitly removes progression and makes escalation difficult to defend.

cues.phrase: no bleeding or heparin-associated reaction is recorded
cues.why: Together with stable hemoglobin/renal function and confirmed dosing, it explicitly rules out reasons for changing or supplementing therapy.

fairness: Continuing treatment is defensible: a persistent duplex abnormality after several days does not by itself establish treatment failure. However, every other supplied observation favors continuing the same treatment, leaving no close competing management error beyond expecting rapid clot disappearance. Too easy for the stated resident target.
Importance: high-yield anticoagulation and avoiding unnecessary filters. Realism: persistent swelling can prompt a repeat study, though the clinical role of this early repeat should be made clear.
suggestions: Retain appropriate safety information, but compare realistic responses to an apparent treatment-response discrepancy rather than supplying a checklist that excludes every reason to change therapy.
If the intended objective is simply that early residual thrombus is not failure, seek explicit basic-role acceptance; do not label it difficult by adding normal results.

title: Investigating oxygen-carrying capacity

cues.phrase: Room-air saturation 98% at rest and 97% during the observed walk; room-air arterial oxygen tension within interval
cues.why: Already supplies reassuring oxygen assessment, directly weakening the repeat blood-gas option.

cues.phrase: without breathlessness or chest pain
cues.why: Further suppresses the cardiopulmonary alternatives while microcytic anemia is the only positive abnormality.

fairness: Iron studies are a defensible assessment of pre-existing and worsened microcytic anemia. No two consequential steps are required: recognize microcytosis and order its familiar initial workup. The normal oxygen measurements are appropriate if distinguishing saturation from content is the objective, but this option set makes them mostly exclusion scaffolding.

Importance: high-yield anemia evaluation. Realism: clinic follow-up is plausible, although a current room-air arterial gas for stable fatigue appears unnecessarily elaborate without another indication.
suggestions: Use a genuine interpretive conflict in anemia testing or postoperative iron assessment that changes management; compare credible hematologic workups rather than unrelated organ investigations.
Avoid adding an arterial gas merely to exclude the arterial-gas distractor. If oxygen-content physiology is the intended concept, ask a consequential physiology decision instead.

title: Tissue sampling after inadequate neck FNA

cues.phrase: Two ultrasound-guided FNAs
cues.why: The repeated failed sampling route makes a third FNA an obvious reuse foil unless its on-site preparation would address a clearly specified prior deficiency.

cues.phrase: behind the internal jugular vein and against the carotid sheath
cues.why: Acts as a risk cue against open excision without establishing that a core needle has a safer feasible path; this can bias the key without resolving safety.

fairness: Recognizing a classification/architecture problem and choosing a tissue route is meaningful. However, suspected lymphoid disease may require architecture and sufficient tissue for full classification; core and excision can both be defensible depending on feasibility and diagnostic requirements. CT depth alone does not establish core as the unique best route.

Importance: useful general-surgery neck-node workup. Realism: an enlarging deep node after two nondiagnostic classifications is plausible, but acquisition safety and pathologist material requirements are decision-critical omissions.
suggestions: Specify whether architecture, additional ancillary material, or both are required, and provide actual imaging evidence of feasible needle and surgical routes.
Compare acquisitions capable of meeting the requirement. Do not imply proximity to vessels is by itself proof that percutaneous core is safer than excision.

title: Perioperative respiratory acid-base trajectory

cues.phrase: a decline in delivered tidal volume during insufflation while the set respiratory rate remained unchanged
cues.why: States the mechanism of reduced ventilation immediately before the only ventilation-increase answer.

cues.phrase: Increase alveolar ventilation; recheck arterial gas
cues.why: The other options maintain or reduce ventilation despite the explicit volume decline and CO2 rise. The initial alkalosis can be ignored.

fairness: Increasing effective ventilation with reassessment is defensible among these options, and the paired gas values are approximately internally coherent. However, the normal-range later pH does not create a close competitor once the mechanism is stated. This is not a difficult mixed-disorder decision.

Importance: high-yield perioperative physiology. Realism: a retrospective anesthetic record is plausible; a live response also requires checking the cause of reduced delivered volume and airway/mechanical issues, not merely changing an abstract ventilation goal.
suggestions: Remove the explanatory ventilator-mechanism sentence if it is not the objective, or provide an actual ventilator record that must be interpreted.
Make the metabolic background consequential to a concrete ventilator/action choice, using credible alternatives that each address the observed deterioration.

title: Reassessing a changing hand burn

cues.phrase: no burn operating service
cues.why: Makes the external surgical-assessment option the only feasible escalation in the stated clinic.

cues.phrase: urgent circumferential eschar-release surgery
cues.why: An anatomically mismatched escalation for a described dorsal-joint burn, with no circumferential constriction or distal compromise described; it is a weak distractor.

fairness: Changing depth findings at functionally important hand joints support renewed burn-center assessment. The key is defensible, but the choice reduces to escalating clearly worsened wound findings versus unchanged care or an unsupported emergency release. Too easy unless explicitly accepted as a safety-recognition exception.

Importance: high-yield recognition and referral. Realism: the initial photo consultation and later in-person reassessment are credible; the exact same-day urgency should receive clinical confirmation rather than be treated as a universal timing rule.
suggestions: Keep the concerning findings and referral threshold visible. Seek explicit safety/basic-role acceptance or compare closer burn-center management decisions supported by adequate findings.
Replace eschar release with a clinically credible competitor at the same stage. Remove the facility sentence if it merely restates why referral is the only possible escalation.

title: Paired treatments for urgent VKA reversal
fairness: The learner must interpret transient INR correction followed by recurrent elevation after potentially unabsorbed oral treatment, then distinguish restoring sustained reversal from repeating immediate factor replacement in a currently stable patient. The emesis and suction are legitimate route/absorption observations; they do not disclose the separate pharmacologic role of vitamin K without knowledge.

Importance: high-yield anticoagulant reversal and avoidance of unnecessary factor products. Realism: credible inpatient record reviewed in clinic. The appropriateness of the exact IV regimen and continued anticoagulation interruption depends on bleeding/thrombotic context not specified; no dose is being endorsed.
suggestions: Preserve the timing, observed emesis, stable hemostasis and no-warfarin-restart information. Confirm the detailed reversal regimen clinically before use; do not generalize this plan to recurrent active major hemorrhage.

title: Rapid VKA factor replacement

cues.phrase: After the first plasma unit he developed rising jugular venous pressure, crackles and increased oxygen needs
cues.why: Specifically undermines the plasma competitor while the task asks for another rapid product. This adds an exclusion to a familiar PCC-selection rule rather than a necessary second inference.

cues.phrase: Thawed plasma for vitamin-K-dependent factor replacement
cues.why: The plasma option is longer and explanatory while both concentrates have concise product labels; wording is not parallel, though this alone does not identify the key.

fairness: Four-factor PCC accompanying IV vitamin K is a defensible choice for the described major warfarin-associated bleeding. The same key would generally follow without the new congestion findings, so that update does not create two-step reasoning. Recombinant factor VII is a weak comparator for routine complete VKA reversal.
Importance: very high-yield emergency reversal. Realism: volume-related deterioration during plasma administration is plausible, but the item does not require its precise diagnosis.
suggestions: Use an actual remaining reversal decision after initial treatment, where interpreting the response changes the product/action, or seek explicit foundational/safety-role acceptance.
Make product labels parallel and avoid using a completed poorly tolerated treatment as the sole plausible alternative.

title: Early nutrition after an extensive burn

cues.phrase: while urgent abdominal assessment proceeds
cues.why: The task pre-announces serious abdominal concern, making pausing feeding the readily guessed cautious answer.

cues.phrase: Vasopressor restarted and increasing
cues.why: Together with falling urine output, distension, tenderness and bloody drainage, stacks unmistakable deterioration against both feeding options.

fairness: Pausing feeds while urgently evaluating the described deterioration is a defensible safety response. The condition need not be precisely diagnosed to choose it; route change and continued feeding are not close competitors in this record. Preserve these red flags rather than hiding them to manufacture difficulty.
Importance: high-yield burn/critical-care nutrition safety. Realism: coherent burn-center course, but this is a safety-recognition question rather than a hard nutrition prescription decision.
suggestions: Seek explicit independent acceptance as an easy safety item, or construct a separate nutrition decision with a genuine, safely specified perfusion/tolerance ambiguity.
Keep urgent assessment in the clinical plan, but avoid a task that announces the concern being tested. Never weaken the deterioration findings simply to keep feeding distractors alive.

title: Planned thoracic injury exposure

cues.phrase: Planned right posterolateral thoracotomy
cues.why: Only this option is labelled 'Planned', flagging it as the obsolete pre-arrest plan in a task explicitly about the last stage.

cues.phrase: Which initial chest exposure best fits the last stage of Nathan Scott's recorded course?
cues.why: The explicit last-stage instruction, paired with the uniquely 'Planned' distractor, advertises abandoning the earlier anatomy-based choice.

fairness: A witnessed recent penetrating-trauma arrest in the resuscitation bay changes the operative objective; initial left anterolateral exposure is defensible among the options. This can be genuine two-step reasoning: recognize the changed stage, then select the resuscitative approach. Median sternotomy is a real exposure but less suitable as the default initial bay approach in this scenario.

Importance: high-yield trauma prioritization and exposure. Realism: the postoperative-clinic record-review wrapper is acceptable if clearly retrospective. The middle-esophageal/azygos findings should remain subordinate to the new arrest; they do not justify a delayed planned repair.
suggestions: Use parallel exposure labels, removing 'Planned' from only one choice. Ask neutrally which exposure the team should use now.
Retain the witnessed-arrest chronology and resuscitation-bay setting because they make the ranking fair; do not remove essential timing to increase difficulty.
